summary: Describes requirements for Securely Available Credentials protocols, which let users securely get their credentials, such as private keys, from different devices.

plainLanguage.summary: Private keys and other credentials usually live on one machine, so a user who wants to send signed email from both a laptop and a phone has to move the key between them. This memo is the checklist that any protocol for doing that safely must meet: the two kinds of solution, the attacks each must withstand, and the rules that apply to both.

questions: what is sacred securely available credentials
how to move private keys between devices
sacred credential server vs direct transfer
subtitle: What a protocol must do to let people move private keys and other credentials safely between their devices.

tldr.problem: Private keys and other credentials sit on one device, so a user who wants signed email from both a laptop and a phone has to move the key, and moving it has to be safe.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements for SACRED protocols: two kinds of solution, a credential server that stores and hands out credentials or a direct transfer between devices, together with a list of vulnerabilities each protocol must address and the general rules that apply to both.
tldr.outcome: The requirements cover the confidentiality of the credential, authentication of the server, replay protection, auditing and denial of service. The memo is Informational, and says the direct-transfer requirements are provisional.

today: RFC 3157 is an Informational memo setting out the requirements for SACRED protocols, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. The memo says the requirements for direct transfer are provisional and that another document will be needed before such a protocol can proceed, and it points to companion documents for the framework and for the protocols themselves. It is read with RFC 2440 for one of the credential formats it requires, OpenPGP.

sections.title: Why Credentials Need to Move
sections.content:
Credentials are information that can be used to establish the identity of an entity, or help that entity communicate securely. They include such things as private keys, trusted roots, tickets, or the private part of a Personal Security Environment, and they support Internet protocols such as S/MIME, IPsec and TLS.

In simple models, users and other entities are provided with credentials and the credentials stay in one place. But the number of devices that can be used to reach the Internet is increasing: desktop computers, laptop computers, wireless phones, pagers, personal digital assistants and other types of device. Many users want to reach private information and secure services from several devices and want the same access from any of them. Credentials also have to be moved between routers when they are upgraded.

The memo's own examples make the point. Mimi generates a public and private key on her desktop computer, gives the public key to a Certification Authority to be included in a certificate, and keeps the private key on her computer. But she may want to send signed email from the desktop when she is in the office and from her laptop when she is on the road, without recipients knowing the difference, so the private key must be available on both devices. Will wants to retrieve and read encrypted email from either his wireless phone or his two-way pager, so he must have the same private key available on both.

It is generally accepted that the private key in these examples must be transferred securely. In the first example it should not be exposed to anyone other than Mimi herself, and ideally it would not be directly exposed to her either. It must also be transferred correctly: to the proper device, and without being corrupted, improperly modified, during the transfer.

The intent is that this value be provided largely independently of the hardware device used to reach the credential and of the type of storage medium the credential is written to. Different storage devices, from desktop or laptop computer memory to a 3.5 inch flexible diskette, a hard disk file, a cell phone or a smart card, have very different security characteristics and often very different protocol handling capabilities. Using SACRED protocols, users will be able to securely move their credentials between different locations, different Internet devices and different storage media as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A private key that never leaves one machine cannot be used from another. The memo's examples are ordinary: signing email from a laptop on the road, or reading encrypted mail on a phone. Moving the key is the point, and moving it safely is the hard part.

sections.title: The Two Ways to Move a Credential
sections.content:
There are at least two different ways to solve the problem of secure credential transfer between devices. One class of solutions uses a credential server as an intermediate node; the other provides direct transfer between devices. A credential server can be likened to a server that sits in front of a repository where credentials can be securely stored for later retrieval, and it is active in the protocol, implementing security enforcing functionality.

Transferring credentials securely from one end device to another is a straightforward two-step process. Users can have their credentials securely uploaded from one device, for example a wireless phone, to the credential server, stored there, and downloaded when needed using another device, for example a two-way pager.

The memo gives three advantages of the credential server approach. It is conceptually clean and straightforward, because there is one protocol for all end devices, with a set of actions to transfer credentials to the server and another set to transfer them from the server, and it has the familiar shape of a client and a server. It provides a place where credentials can be securely stored for arbitrary lengths of time, so a hardware failure is less likely to destroy them permanently. And the server may be able to enforce a uniform security policy, which matters where credentials are issued by an organisation for its own purposes rather than created by the end user.

There are disadvantages too. It may be expensive to maintain and run, particularly with stringent requirements on availability and reliability, and for a large community of users. And the server has to be trusted in some sense, and introduces a point of potential vulnerability: at a minimum, someone with access to it can delete credentials and thus deny the service to system users.

Some users prefer a different class of solution, in which credentials are transferred directly from one device to another, with no intermediary element that processes or has any understanding of the credentials. The memo's example is Mimi sending a message from her wireless phone and retrieving it on her two-way pager: the bits cross the wireless phone network to a base station, over the wired phone network to a message server run by the wireless operator, over the Internet to a message server run by the paging operator, and then to a base station and finally to the pager. To all the devices except the phone and the pager, what is transferred is an uninterpreted and unprocessed set of bits, and no security-related decisions are made at any intermediate node.

Direct transfer is potentially more complex, owing to the large number of devices and formats that may have to be supported and because each device may have to behave as both a client and a server. The memo believes both classes of solution are useful in certain environments, so the framework has to define solutions for both.

The framework requirements follow. F1: the framework MUST support both credential server and direct solutions. F2: the two SHOULD use the same technology as far as possible. F3: the framework MUST allow for protocols which support different user authentication schemes, since it is often more secure to reuse an existing scheme than to manage a whole new set of passwords, and not all mobile devices can carry out asymmetric cryptography. F4: the details of the actual credential type or format MUST be opaque to the protocol, though not to processing within the protocol's peers, so the protocol MUST NOT depend on the internal structure of any credential type or format; there is no single standard format for credentials today and this is not likely to change, so widely deployed formats such as PGP and PKCS#12 have to be supported. F5: the framework MUST allow use of different transports, because different devices allow different transport layer possibilities, for example current WAP 1.x devices do not support TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Either a server keeps the credential and hands it out when a device asks, or the credential travels straight from one device to another. The server is simpler to build but becomes a target and a single point of failure. The framework has to allow both.

sections.title: Vulnerabilities and the General Rules
sections.content:
The memo first lists the vulnerabilities a SACRED protocol SHOULD offer protection against, and says that any protocol claiming to meet the requirements MUST explicitly indicate how, or whether, it offers protection for each. A passive attacker can watch all packets on the network and later carry out a dictionary attack. An attacker can attempt to masquerade as a credential server, to get a client to reveal information that allows for a later dictionary attack, or to get a client to decrypt a chosen ciphertext and make use of the resulting plaintext, for example using the plaintext from the decryption of a random string as a DSA private key. An attacker could overwrite a repository entry, so that when a user later uses what they think is a good credential they expose information about their password. An attacker can copy a credential server's repository and carry out a dictionary attack, or masquerade as a client to get a server to reveal information that allows for a later dictionary attack. An attacker can persuade a server that a successful login has occurred even if it has not, or overwrite someone else's credentials on the server during an upload. With password-based authentication, an attacker can force a password change to a known or weak password, attempt a man-in-the-middle attack, or exploit a user entering a password instead of a name. An attacker could also attempt various denial-of-service attacks.

The general requirements apply to all secure credential transfer solutions. G1: credential transfer both to and from a device MUST be supported. G2: credentials MUST NOT be forced by the protocol to be present in cleartext at any device other than the end user's. G3: the protocol SHOULD ensure that all transferred credentials are authenticated in some way, for example digitally signed or MAC-ed. G4: the protocol MUST support a range of cryptographic algorithms, including symmetric and asymmetric algorithms, hash algorithms and MAC algorithms. G5: the protocol MUST allow the use of various credential types and formats, such as X.509, PGP and PKCS12. G6: one mandatory to support credential format MUST be defined, and G7: one mandatory to support user authentication scheme MUST be defined. G8: the protocol MAY allow credentials to be labelled with a text handle, outside the credential, to allow the end user to select among a set of credentials or to name a particular credential. G9: full internationalization support is REQUIRED, via UTF8 support. G10: it is desirable that the protocol be able to support privacy, that is, anonymity for the client. G11: transferred credentials MAY incorporate timing information, for example a time to live value determining the maximum time for which the credential is usable following transfer or download.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo lists twelve attacks a protocol should resist, from an eavesdropper who records the traffic to an attacker who replaces a stored credential with one of their own. The general rules follow: the credential must never appear in the clear on anyone else's machine, and it must be authenticated in transit.

sections.title: The Extra Rules for Each Kind of Solution
sections.content:
Solutions with a credential server take on extra requirements. Credential downloads to an end user and upload to the credential server MUST be supported. Credentials MUST only be downloadable following user authentication, or else only in a format that requires completion of user authentication for deciphering. It MUST be possible to ensure the authenticity of a credential during upload, and different end user devices MAY be used to download, upload and manage the same set of credentials.

Credential servers SHOULD be authenticated to the user for all operations except download, although that requirement can be ignored if the credential format itself is strongly protected, since the only risk then is user confusion. It SHOULD be possible to authenticate the credential server to the user as part of a download operation, and the user SHOULD only have to enter a single secret value in order to download and use a credential. Sharing of secrets across multiple servers MAY be possible, so that penetration of some servers does not expose the private parts of a credential, which the memo calls an m-from-n operation. The protocol MAY support away-from-home operation, where the user enters both a name and a domain, for example RoamingStephen@baltimore.ie, and the domain can be used to locate the user's credential server.

The protocol MUST provide operations allowing users to manage their credentials stored on the server, for example to retrieve a list of them, to add credentials and to delete credentials. Client-initiated authentication information, such as a password change, MUST be supported, and the user SHOULD be able to retrieve a list of accesses and changes to their credentials. The protocol MUST support user self-enrollment, so that a previously unknown user can upload a credential without requiring manual operator intervention, and it MUST NOT prevent bulk initializing of a credential server's repository. Finally, the protocol SHOULD require minimal client configuration.

The direct transfer requirements are provisional: the memo says the full set has not been elucidated, and that an additional requirements document, or a modification of this one, will be required before a direct-transfer protocol can proceed. As it stands there are two. D1: it SHOULD be possible for the receiving device to authenticate that the credential package indeed came from the purported sending device. D2: so that a sender knows a credential has been received, it SHOULD be possible for the receiving device to send an acknowledgment of receipt back to the sending device, and for the sending device to authenticate that acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: A credential server has to check the user before releasing anything, must let the user manage and list what is stored, and must support users enrolling themselves. For direct transfer, the two rules are that the receiver can prove where the credential came from, and that the sender can prove it arrived.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mobile credentials will never be as secure as a pure hardware-based solution, because of potential attacks through the operating system of the end-user device, though the memo says an acceptable level of security may be accomplished through some simple means, and that the level may be improved over password encrypted files. The platforms credentials are downloaded to usually cannot be regarded as tamper-resistant, so it is not too hard to analyse the contents of their memories. Storage of private keys, even if they are encrypted, on a credential server will be unacceptable in some environments. And replacement of installed or downloaded SACRED client software with a Trojan horse program will always be possible, and such a program could email the username and password to the program's author.

On auditing, the memo says implementations should carefully audit events that may be security relevant. Credential server implementations should audit all operations and include information about the time and source of the operation, such as an IP address, the claimed identity of the client, the type and result of the operation and possibly other operation specific information. They should take care not to include security sensitive information in the audit trail, especially not sensitive authentication information, and it may be sensible to mask the claimed identity so that a user who enters her password in a username field does not have it appear in clear in the audit trail. Alerts and account locking, in particular following repeated authentication failures, are also sensible, though out of scope for protocol development.

Credential servers are major targets. Someone who attacks one might gain access to the credentials of a number of users, unless those credentials are sufficiently protected, and might substitute credentials of users, for example providing a user with a trusted root credential that the attacker controls. A credential server is also a major target for denial of service, and servers that do lots of expensive cryptographic operations are especially vulnerable, since it might not take very many operations to bring the service to an unacceptable level. Great care should therefore be taken in designing systems that use credential servers to protect against these attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The device that holds the key can be read, and a program on it can steal anything it can reach, so a software credential is never as safe as one in a smart card. The server is the other weak point: it holds other people's keys, and it can be attacked or simply overloaded. Both need careful design and careful logging of what happened.

viz.caption: TWO WAYS TO MOVE A CREDENTIAL

left.title: Credential server
left.desc: The credential is uploaded to a server that stores it and hands it back on download, after the user authenticates.

right.title: Direct transfer
right.desc: The credential goes straight to the other device, with no intermediary that interprets it.

items.title: Passive eavesdropping
items.text: An attacker records the traffic and runs a dictionary attack later.

items.title: Fake server
items.text: An attacker poses as the credential server and collects material for a dictionary attack.

items.title: Chosen ciphertext
items.text: An attacker gets the client to decrypt a chosen value and use it as a key.

items.title: Overwritten repository entry
items.text: An attacker replaces a stored credential so the user later leaks their password.

items.title: Copied repository
items.text: An attacker copies the server's store and attacks it offline.

items.title: Fake client
items.text: An attacker poses as the client and collects material from the server.

items.title: Forced password change
items.text: An attacker forces the password to be reset to a known or weak value.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: An attacker makes the server unavailable or floods it with expensive operations.

viz.caption: THE GENERAL PROTOCOL REQUIREMENTS AS PRINTED IN THE RFC

data.title: Requirements G1 to G11
data.code:
G1.      Credential transfer both to and from a device MUST be
         supported.
G2.      Credentials MUST NOT be forced by the protocol to be present
         in cleartext at any device other than the end user's.
G3.      The protocol SHOULD ensure that all transferred credentials
         be authenticated in some way (e.g., digitally signed or
         MAC-ed).
G4.      The protocol MUST support a range of cryptographic
         algorithms, including symmetric and asymmetric algorithms,
         hash algorithms, and MAC algorithms.
G5.      The protocol MUST allow the use of various credential types
         and formats (e.g., X.509, PGP, PKCS12, ...).
G6.      One mandatory to support credential format MUST be defined.
G7.      One mandatory to support user authentication scheme MUST be
         defined.
G8.      The protocol MAY allow credentials to be labeled with a text
         handle, (outside the credential), to allow the end user to
         select amongst a set of credentials or to name a particular
         credential.
G9.      Full I18N support is REQUIRED (via UTF8 support) [RFC2277].
G10.     It is desirable that the protocol be able to support
         privacy, that is, anonymity for the client.
G11.     Transferred credentials MAY incorporate timing information,
         for example a "time to live" value determining the maximum
         time for which the credential is to be usable following
         transfer/download.
